title: SAUL WAS DESPERATE FOR AN ANSWER FROM GOD. SO HE WENT TO A MEDIUM IN THE DARK.
paragraphs:
SAUL WAS DESPERATE FOR AN ANSWER FROM GOD. SO HE WENT TO A MEDIUM IN THE DARK.
The terrifying story of the woman at Endor is not really about how to contact the dead. It is about what can happen when a heart wants an answer from God more than it wants God Himself.
There is something almost unbearable about the sentence.
God did not answer him.
Not because Saul had never known God.
That would make the story easier.
Saul knew what it was to be chosen.
He knew what it was to have Samuel speak the word of the LORD over his life. He knew what it was to stand among ordinary men and suddenly discover that God had placed a kingdom on his shoulders.
He had experienced victory.
Anointing.
Prophetic confirmation.
The Spirit of God had come upon him.
Once, Saul looked like the beginning of something beautiful.
And now...
he was standing in the dark.
Terrified.
Desperate.
Disguised.
Looking for a woman he himself had once driven out of the land.
A medium.
Because heaven seemed silent.
And if you have ever prayed until your throat felt empty...
if you have ever begged God for direction and received no immediate explanation...

if you have ever watched the deadline approach, the relationship collapse, the diagnosis arrive, the money disappear, the opportunity close, the person walk away, or the future become terrifyingly unclear...
then be careful before you look down on Saul.
You may have never walked to Endor.
But desperation has its own Endors.
And some of them are only one frightened decision away.
The Philistines had gathered for war.
Saul saw their army, and Scripture does not soften what happened inside him.
The Hebrew says:
וַיִּרָא וַיֶּחֱרַד לִבּוֹ מְאֹד
Vayyira, vayyecherad libbo me’od.
He was afraid, and his heart trembled greatly.
This was not mild anxiety.
The king was unraveling.
Then comes one of the darkest sentences in Saul’s life:
וַיִּשְׁאַל שָׁאוּל בַּיהוָה וְלֹא עָנָהוּ יְהוָה
Vayyish’al Sha’ul ba-YHWH, velo ‘anahu YHWH.
“Saul inquired of the LORD, but the LORD did not answer him.”
Not by dreams.
Not by the Urim.
Not by the prophets.
Nothing.
Silence.
And this is where the story becomes frighteningly personal.
Because silence reveals things.
When God does not give us the answer we want when we want it, we discover whether we were seeking God...
or merely seeking relief.
There is an enormous difference between wanting God’s will and wanting God to approve ours.

Saul had spent years resisting the voice of God, rationalizing disobedience, preserving what God told him to destroy, fearing people, protecting his position, hunting David, and repeatedly moving farther from surrendered obedience.
Now he wanted guidance.
But guidance cannot be separated from surrender.
Saul wanted another word while his life was still haunted by the words he had already refused to obey.
That should make every believer uncomfortable.
Because sometimes we cry,
“God, speak to me!”
while an old command is still lying ignored at our feet.
Forgive them.
No.
End the secret sin.
Not yet.
Tell the truth.
That would cost too much.
Repent.
Maybe tomorrow.
Stop returning to what is destroying you.
But Lord, just give me a sign...
We can become obsessed with receiving new revelation while resisting old obedience.
Saul’s tragedy did not begin at Endor.
Endor was simply where years of compromise finally became visible.
Long before Saul walked into that night, Samuel had confronted him with words that still pierce the conscience:
“To obey is better than sacrifice.”
Saul wanted the kingdom without surrender.
He wanted God’s power without God’s government.
He wanted divine confirmation without complete obedience.
Eventually desperation exposed him.
And that is when Saul said something astonishing:
בַּקְּשׁוּ־לִי אֵשֶׁת בַּעֲלַת־אוֹב
Baqqeshu-li ’eshet ba‘alat-’ov.
“Find me a woman who is a medium.”

The Hebrew expression בַּעֲלַת־אוֹב — ba‘alat-’ov describes a woman associated with or possessing an ’ov, a term used in the Old Testament in connection with forbidden attempts to consult the dead or spirits.
And Saul knew it was forbidden.
That makes the scene even darker.
Earlier in the very chapter, Scripture tells us that Saul himself had removed the mediums and spiritists from the land.
He knew.
He had enforced the prohibition.
God’s Law was not unclear about occult consultation. Israel had been explicitly forbidden from turning to mediums, spiritists, divination, and attempts to consult the dead.
Yet fear can make a person seek privately what he once condemned publicly.
Read that again.
Because that is not merely Saul’s problem.
A person can preach against something and secretly hunger for it.
A person can warn others about sin while slowly negotiating with the same sin behind closed doors.
A person can look spiritually strong in daylight and become someone completely different when night falls.
And Saul literally went at night.
He removed his royal clothing.
He disguised himself.
He took two men with him.
And Scripture says:
וַיָּבֹאוּ אֶל־הָאִשָּׁה לָיְלָה
They came to the woman by night.
What a picture.
Israel’s king...
hiding his identity...
walking through darkness...
looking for forbidden guidance...
because he could no longer bear the silence.
There are sins that love darkness because darkness makes us believe nobody can see the contradiction.
The hidden browser.
The deleted conversation.
The second account.
The secret relationship.
The private addiction.
The horoscope you insist is “just entertainment.”
The psychic reading you call curiosity.
The spiritual practice you know does not belong to Christ.
The compromise nobody at church knows about.
The bitterness you have learned to hide beneath Christian vocabulary.
The sin you keep renaming because calling it what Scripture calls it would require repentance.
You may change clothes.
You may delete history.
You may fool your family.
You may fool your pastor.
You may even fool yourself.
But you cannot disguise yourself before God.
Saul entered that house pretending not to be Saul.
But heaven knew exactly who had walked through the door.
And perhaps somebody reading this has been doing the same thing.
Not consulting a medium.
Something subtler.
You still post Bible verses.
Still say “God is good.”
Still know when to raise your hands.
Still know Christian language.
Still look normal.
But somewhere inside, you know you have been walking farther into the night.
And the most dangerous part is that you still want God to answer you without touching the thing you refuse to surrender.
Saul asked the woman to bring up Samuel.
What follows has generated centuries of discussion.

The narrative itself repeatedly calls the figure Samuel, and the message given to Saul is consistent with judgment previously announced through Samuel: the kingdom had been torn from Saul, David would receive it, and Saul and his sons were facing death.

Christians have proposed different explanations for exactly what occurred—whether God sovereignly permitted Samuel himself to appear despite the forbidden ritual, or whether the event should be understood differently.
We should not pretend Scripture tells us more than it does.
But we must not miss what Scripture makes unmistakably clear:
Saul’s action was rebellion, not a model for spiritual guidance.
The Bible never presents necromancy as an acceptable way to seek God.
In fact, 1 Chronicles later gives the inspired verdict on Saul’s death: his unfaithfulness included consulting a medium for guidance rather than faithfully seeking the LORD.
The point of Endor is not, “Here is how the supernatural works.”
The point is much more terrifying:
Look what desperation becomes when it is separated from obedience.
And here is the irony.
Saul finally heard a voice.
But it did not give him the escape he wanted.
It confirmed the judgment he feared.
He had crossed forbidden ground searching for another answer, only to encounter the consequence of refusing the answers God had already given him.
When Saul heard what was coming, Scripture says he fell immediately.
Full length.
On the ground.
The king who once stood taller than everyone in Israel was now lying helpless on the floor of a medium’s house.
No crown could help him.
No army could comfort him.
No disguise could protect him.
No forbidden spiritual experience could rewrite what rebellion had produced.
And there, lying in the darkness, Saul becomes a warning to every human heart:
You can spend so long running from God that eventually you become desperate for the comfort of the God whose authority you rejected.
That sentence hurts because many of us recognize ourselves in smaller ways.
We want God when the marriage is breaking.
God when the doctor calls.
God when the money runs out.
God when the child is in trouble.
God when panic attacks at 2:00 a.m.
God when consequences finally knock.
And thank God—we absolutely should run to Him in those moments.
But there is a difference between running to God in repentance and demanding that God rescue us while we continue protecting our rebellion.
Saul wanted information.
What he needed was surrender.
And maybe that is what you need too.
Not another sign.
Not another prophecy video.
Not another person telling you what you desperately want to hear.
Not another spiritual shortcut.
Not another attempt to manipulate tomorrow.
Maybe what you need tonight is to fall before Jesus Christ and finally tell Him the truth.
“Lord, I have been running.”
“I have been compromising.”
“I have been asking You to bless what You told me to leave.”
“I have been searching everywhere except where You told me to stand.”
“I have been afraid.”
“I have been hiding.”
“I need mercy.”
And here is where Saul’s story makes us ache for the Gospel.
Because Saul’s story shows us where rebellion leads.
But Jesus shows us what grace can do with rebels who repent.
The Bible does not tell us that Saul’s visit to Endor became a beautiful repentance story.
We should not rewrite Saul’s ending into something Scripture does not say.
But Saul’s tragedy makes the mercy offered in Christ shine even brighter.
Because another Saul eventually appears in Scripture.
Saul of Tarsus.
A violent persecutor.
A man breathing threats against Christ’s people.
A man convinced he was right while fighting against the very Messiah Israel had been waiting for.
And Jesus stopped him on another road.
Not the road to Endor.
The road to Damascus.
“Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?”
One Saul kept hardening himself against God’s word until darkness swallowed his kingdom.
Another Saul was confronted by the risen Christ, humbled, transformed, and eventually became Paul—the apostle who would proclaim the grace he once opposed.
That contrast should shake us.
Your scandal does not have to become your ending.
Your worst chapter does not have authority over the blood of Jesus.
Your hidden sin is serious.
Your rebellion is serious.
Your compromise is serious.
Your occult involvement is serious.
Your disobedience is serious.
But Jesus Christ is not asking you to clean yourself enough to become worthy of approaching Him.
He calls you to repent and believe.
The cross exists precisely because sin cannot be treated casually.
At Calvary, Christ bore judgment for sinners.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And forgiveness is not found in hiding from the truth but in coming into the light and trusting the One who paid for sinners with His own blood.

If you have been involved in mediums, psychics, séances, spirit guides, occult practices, divination, or any spiritual practice contrary to Scripture, Christianity does not tell you to live terrified that darkness owns you forever.
It tells you to turn from it and turn to Christ.
Renounce what Scripture forbids.
Confess your sin.
Destroy whatever keeps pulling you back.
Seek mature biblical pastoral help where needed.
And place your confidence not in rituals, objects, mediums, signs, or spiritual experiences...
but in Jesus Christ.
Because the answer to forbidden spiritual darkness is not stronger superstition.
It is Christ.
The answer to guilt is Christ.
The answer to condemnation for those who are in Him is Christ.
The answer to the sinner who finally whispers, “I have gone too far” is not pretending sin never mattered.
It is the crucified and risen Savior whose grace is greater than anything you can bring to His feet.
Peter failed.
Christ restored him.
The thief was dying beside Jesus with nothing left to offer.
Christ received him.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Christ transformed him.
The Gospel is filled with people whose stories should have ended in scandal...
but grace interrupted.
That is why our message remains:
Not because Jesus edits sin until it looks harmless.
He does something infinitely greater.
He forgives sinners.
He makes the spiritually dead alive.
He brings people out of darkness.
He transforms rebels into disciples.
He turns shame into testimony.
He takes the person who has been hiding and teaches them to walk in the light.
And maybe this article found you while you are standing at your own Endor.
You know the door.
You know the compromise.
You know what you are about to do.
You know what you have already done.
You know the conversation you keep returning to.
You know the secret.
You know the habit.
You know the spiritual curiosity that has begun pulling you somewhere Scripture told you not to go.
Please hear this before you take another step into the dark:
You do not need Endor. You need Jesus.
Do not let God’s apparent silence convince you that disobedience has become permission.
Do not interpret waiting as abandonment.
Do not allow fear to become your theologian.
Do not let desperation choose your master.
When you cannot hear God clearly, cling to what He has already spoken.
Stay with Scripture.
Stay in prayer.
Stay among faithful believers.
Obey the truth you already know.
Wait.
Trust.
Repent where repentance is necessary.
And keep your eyes on Christ.
Sometimes faith is not receiving an immediate explanation.
Sometimes faith is refusing to walk into forbidden darkness while you wait for the morning.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every detail. But you do need to stop pretending with God.

And if Christ has already brought you out of a darkness you thought would destroy you, tell someone what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the light another frightened person desperately needs tonight.
Send it privately to the person who has been searching everywhere for answers.

Invite your family, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow too. Sometimes one faithful share puts truth in front of someone who would never have searched for it themselves.
It cannot.
Not because supporting a ministry proves that you love Jesus.
Only God knows the heart.
And not because giving money earns blessing, salvation, forgiveness, or spiritual status.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Come to Jesus.
Not to us.
Not to a brand.
Not to a personality.
Not to a medium.
Not to the dead.
Not to another sign.
To Jesus.
If God feels silent tonight, do not go looking for another voice in the darkness.
Open His Word.
Bring Him your fear.
Bring Him your anger.
Bring Him your questions.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the thing you swore nobody would ever know.
Bring Him your whole ruined, frightened, exhausted heart.
And repent.
Because the Savior who died for sinners is alive.
The tomb is empty.
Grace is still being offered.
And while Saul walked into the darkness desperately searching for a voice...
you have been invited to walk out of yours following the voice of the Shepherd who laid down His life for His sheep.
Remember this when your own night becomes frightening:
Never let one silent night convince you to abandon the God who is still writing your morning.
